newsitem.title: EGYPT: Nile cruiser capsize; six bodies found, 11 missing.
newsitem.headline: Nile cruiser capsize; six bodies found, 11 missing.

text.p: Egyptian frogmen and other rescue workers retrieved the bodies of six east European tourists from a capsized Nile cruiser on Friday and officials said they feared another 11 people had also drowned.
Eight Czech and Slovak tourists and three Egyptians were still missing, believed trapped in the cabins of the cruiser, the Amira Jihan, which tipped over in a freak storm on Thursday.
The boat was lying on its side, half-submerged and grounded on a sand bank in the middle of the Nile off the village of Qalh al-Jabal, about 580 km (360 miles) south of Cairo.
More than 100 people -- about 63 tourists and 48 Egyptians -- survived the capsize and the tourists, mostly Czechs and Slovaks, have gone to the nearby tourist resort of Luxor.
Officials at the scene said they doubted any of the missing people would still be alive in the cabins after almost 24 hours, though some may have found pockets of air.
"We have lost hope of finding anyone alive but we are trying to pull the bodies out and find a way to comfort the survivors," Mohamed Youssef, chairman of Luxor town council, told Reuters.
Frogmen continued to dive on Friday afternoon in search of the other missing. They were breaking into cabins one by one and checking for bodies.

Officials at the scene named three dead as a Czech couple, Ian Biovsky and his wife Juka, and a Polish woman, Iren Szendziolorz, whose husband Teodor was among the survivors. The identities of the others were not available.
Ashraf Bennan, an Egyptian tour guide who was on the boat at the time, said Biovsky had celebrated his 50th birthday with a party on the morning of the accident.
He said the boat suddenly listed some time between 3.30 and 4 p.m. on Thursday, at an hour when many of the tourists were resting in their cabins after lunch.
"I was in the restaurant on the lower deck talking to a friend of mine when I felt the boat lean," he told Reuters.
"I ran up quickly and the pressure of the water broke the windows behind me. We pulled as many people as we could out of the cabins but the only tools we had were ropes," he added.

Natasha Kasalova from Prague, rescued with her husband, was in the restaurant. "The flood became the wall and the wall the floor. It was all tables and chairs and we were up to our necks in water. The tour guide saved us. He carried us and pulled us up with a rope," she said.

Villagers in Qalh al-Jabal said the winds had been unusally strong on Thursday afternoon, bending palm trees along the Nile. The current was also in full spate because of heavy rains in Ethiopia this year.
Youssef said such storms were very rare, occurring once in 10 years or even less frequently.

Bennan and the Interior Ministry in Cairo said the boat was carrying 77 tourists and 51 Egyptians -- five tour guides and 46 crew. The ministry said the tourists were either Czechs or Slovaks but Bennan said there were three Poles.
The cruiser was making the popular trip from Aswan to Luxor, passing by the Pharaonic temples of Kom Ombo, Edfu and Esna.

It was the worst accident on a cruiser for many years, though disasters with local ferries are more common. Dozens drowned in September when an overloaded ferry capsized while bringing them from a funeral. That accident took place further north, in the province of Minya.
